title: Ordering a first-match rule list: enumeration of all k! orders vs dynamic programming over subsets of rules
problem_statement: Given k rules and m items, where for every item i and rule r a flag match[i][r] says whether r matches i and a non-negative integer cost[i][r] is the price paid if r is the FIRST rule of the order that matches i, and a non-negative integer default[i] is paid by an item that no rule matches, find an order of the k rules that minimises the total price of all items. Output the minimum total price and an order attaining it (ties: any optimal order). Every item is captured by exactly one rule (the first matching one in the order) or by the default, as in a first-match rule list, decision list or packet filter.

input.parameter: n = k = number of rules. The number of items m is a second parameter: arbitrary in V1, m = k in the V2 family.
input.size_measure: 2km + m integers (the match flags, the costs, the defaults). The V2 family has m = k items, so Theta(k^2) integers.

algorithms.name: enumeration of all orders
algorithms.idea: Try all k! orders of the rules. For each order, scan the order for every item until its first matching rule and add that rule's cost (or the default if no rule matches); keep the cheapest order.
algorithms.time_complexity: O(k! k m): k! orders, at most k match tests per item, one addition per item. On the V2 family (m = k, item i matched by rules i and i+1 mod k) exactly k! (k+1)(k+3)/3 - 1 counted operations = Theta(k! k^2) = Theta(k! k m): k! k(k+1)/3 truth tests (the earlier of an item's two rules stands on average at position (k+1)/3 of a random order: P(min >= j) = C(k-j+1, 2)/C(k, 2), summed over j = 1..k this is C(k+1, 3)/C(k, 2)), k! k additions and k! - 1 comparisons (none for the first order).
algorithms.correctness: Exhaustive: every order is evaluated with the first-match rule, so the minimum over all orders is returned.

algorithms.name: dynamic programming over subsets of rules
algorithms.idea: If the set S of rules placed so far is known, placing rule r next captures exactly the items matched by r and by no rule of S, whatever the order inside S. So best[S + {r}] = min over the last rule r of best[S] + gain(S, r), with gain(S, r) = sum of cost[i][r] over the items matched by r and by no rule of S. For each S one pass over the items collects gain(S, r) for all r at once.
algorithms.pseudocode:
mask[i] = sum of match[i][r] << r; rules[i] = [r : match[i][r]]
best[{}] = 0
for S = 0 .. 2^k - 1 (as integers, so subsets come first):
  gain = [0] * k
  for each item i with mask[i] & S == 0: for r in rules[i]: gain[r] += cost[i][r]
  for r not in S: best[S | {r}] = min(best[S | {r}], best[S] + gain[r])   (remember the minimising r)
return best[all] + sum of default[i] over items with no matching rule, and the order rebuilt from the remembered rules
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(2^k (k + m)) on every input: per subset m capture tests and k - |S| transitions; an item matched by t >= 1 rules is uncaptured for 2^(k-t) subsets and then adds t costs, and t 2^(k-t) <= 2^(k-1). Exactly 3k^2 + (7k - 2) 2^(k-1) + 2 counted operations on the V2 family (k >= 2): 3km = 3k^2 for building the rule lists (k truth tests per item) and the masks (k shifts and k additions per item); 2k 2^k for the capture tests (an & and a truth test per item and subset); k 2^(k-1) gain additions (each item is uncaptured for the 2^(k-2) subsets avoiding its two rules and then adds 2 costs); k 2^(k-1) transition additions; k 2^(k-1) - 2^k + 1 comparisons (a subset T is reached |T| times, the first arrival is stored without comparison); 1 final addition.
algorithms.space_complexity: Theta(2^k) table entries (best value and last rule per subset).
algorithms.correctness: Standard: this is the dynamic program of Yee, Dahan, Hauser & Orlin 2007 (Algorithm 2), whose correctness rests on their Propositions 2 and 3, stated for weighted lexicographic fitting (costs 0 or w per item). Their argument uses only the fact that whether a rule captures an item depends on the set of rules placed before it, not on their order, so it carries over unchanged to arbitrary costs. In the notation here: Claim: best[S] is the minimum, over the orders of the rules in S, of the total cost of the items captured by S (those matched by some rule of S). Induction on |S|: in an order of S whose last rule is r, the items captured by r are those matched by r and by no rule of S - {r}, and they pay cost[i][r] whatever the order of S - {r}; the remaining captured items are captured by S - {r} and pay best[S - {r}] at the cheapest. Hence best[S] = min over r in S of best[S - {r}] + gain(S - {r}, r). For S = all rules, the items not captured pay their defaults, which do not depend on the order. The remembered minimising rules rebuild an optimal order backwards. The recurrence over (set placed so far, next element) is that of Held & Karp 1962, to which Yee et al. compare their algorithm, and of the vertex-ordering framework of Bodlaender et al. 2012. The principle that orders of the same set capture the same items is also the equivalent-support bound of CORELS (Angelino et al.: Theorem 15 and Corollary 16, the symmetry-aware map), stated there for learning certifiably optimal rule lists.

shape.note: the closed form holds for k >= 2; a constant-coefficient recurrence of order 5 ((x-2)^2 (x-1)^3) needs 16 terms

relationship: Factorial -> single exponential: enumeration O(k! k m) -> subset DP Theta(2^k (k + m)), on the V2 family Theta(k! k^2) vs Theta(k 2^k). Both stay exponential in k. Yee et al. 2007 present the subset DP as turning a search over n! orders into a search over 2^n subsets. The problem is NP-hard (decision version NP-complete), so a polynomial algorithm would imply P = NP; hence primary T6 with T8 for the verified improvement. Reduction (proved in caveats, tested in the experiment): FEEDBACK ARC SET, NP-complete by Karp 1972, maps to items matched by exactly two rules with costs 0 and 1; this is the reduction of Schmitt & Martignon 2006 (Theorem 5) for lexicographic cue orders. With at most two matching rules per item the problem is exactly the linear ordering problem (NP-hard, Grötschel, Jünger & Reinelt 1984).

sources.note: CORELS: rule lists with first-match semantics; Theorem 15 (equivalent support bound) and Corollary 16 (permutation bound) keep only the best ordering of each set of antecedents (the symmetry-aware map); theorem numbers as in the arXiv version.

verification.method: V1: the validator runs k = 0..7, 9 and 11, 6 instances per size: random items (match probability 0.2-0.7, m = 0..2k+2), feedback-arc-set reductions of random weighted digraphs, the cyclic V2 family with random costs, all-pairs (linear ordering) instances with single-rule items, items matched by no rule or by every rule with zero costs (ties) and duplicated items, few-rule instances with costs up to 10^6; costs at non-matching positions are random integers that must be ignored; the enumeration runs up to k = 7, the DP on every size. check is independent of both implementations: it requires a permutation, recomputes the order's cost from rule positions (the matching rule of smallest position), rejects a cost below the lower bound sum_i min_{r in M_i} cost[i][r] (plus defaults) and certifies a cost equal to it, and otherwise computes the optimum by a depth-first branch and bound over order prefixes (exact for k <= 7; above, a budget of 300 000 nodes, after which an improving move of one rule proves non-optimality and anything else is undecided). experiments/2026-10-07_first_match_checks.py: (1) the exact V2 counts against the closed forms below; (2) agreement and oracle on extra instances k = 0..12; (3) the feedback-arc-set reduction on 300 random weighted digraphs with at most 14 arcs: the optimum equals the brute-force minimum feedback arc set weight, and for every order the reduced cost equals the weight of the backward arcs; (4) items matching at most two rules: the cost of every order equals a constant plus the forward weight of a linear ordering instance; (5) oracle control with deliberately wrong outputs (cost +- 1, worse orders with honest or optimal cost, repeated, missing or extra rules, the cost of the reversed order, defaults ignored, wrong types). V2 (exact counts): generate_scaling gives the cyclic family (m = k, item i matched by rules i and i+1 mod k, costs drawn from rng) with CountingInt entries, which count every truth test, comparison, +, -, <<, &, | on entry-derived values; the implementations are unchanged. Enumeration: exactly k! (k+1)(k+3)/3 - 1 (checked for k = 2..8); fit against that form on k = 4..8; rivals k! k, k! k^3 and k 2^k. Subset DP: exactly 3k^2 + (7k - 2) 2^(k-1) + 2 (checked for k = 2..18); fit on k = 6..14; rivals k^2 2^k (the cost of scanning all items for every pair (S, r)), 2^k, k! and 3^k. The counts do not depend on the drawn costs. No counted operation happens inside a CPython built-in such as sorted, min or max (sum() adds CountingInt values through their own __add__/__radd__).

caveats: NP-hardness, by the reduction of Schmitt & Martignon 2006 (Theorem 5), stated there for the cue orders of lexicographic strategies (each arc becomes a pair of objects that only the arc's two cues discriminate, one deciding it correctly and the other incorrectly), from FEEDBACK ARC SET (decision: does a digraph D = (V, A) have a set of at most K arcs whose removal leaves it acyclic?): take the vertices as rules and, for every arc u -> v, an item matched by u and v with cost 0 for u and 1 for v. An order pays 1 exactly for the arcs that point backwards in it. The backward arcs of any order form a feedback arc set, and for any feedback arc set F a topological order of D - F has only arcs of F pointing backwards, so the minimum total price equals the minimum feedback arc set size; the decision version of the first-match problem is in NP (an order is a certificate) and hence NP-complete. Arcs with integer weights give the weighted version. Arithmetic is unit cost; all numbers are sums of at most m input costs. The enumeration's cost depends on where the matching rules stand: an item matched by every rule costs one test per order, an item matched by none k tests; O(k! k m) is its worst case. What is counted differs slightly by algorithm: the enumeration does truth tests, additions and comparisons; the DP also builds masks with << and + and tests them with &. Loop control, subset arithmetic on plain integers (S & bit, S | bit) and list bookkeeping are not counted; in the DP they are of the same order as the counted operations (k - |S| bit tests per subset for the transitions). Additions and comparisons in which both operands are plain integers are not counted: in the DP a gain that no uncaptured item contributes to stays a plain 0, and on inputs where best[S] + gain[r] has two plain operands (only for S = {} with gain 0) one addition and one comparison are not seen; on the V2 family every such operand is input-derived, which the closed form checks. The V1 oracle is exact for k <= 7 and, above, for the instances on which the lower bound is attained or branch and bound finishes within its budget; elsewhere it applies necessary conditions only.
notes: Literature: MaxDL (Chakravarthy et al. 2008) is this problem with 0/1 costs: rules carry labels, cost[i][r] = 0 if rule r gives item i its correct label and 1 otherwise, and every default is 1, so minimising the total price maximises the number of correctly labelled items. Weighted lexicographic fitting (Yee et al. 2007, Proposition 3) is the case in which an item is a pair of profiles with an observed preference and a weight w, a rule is an aspect that matches the pair iff it tells the two profiles apart, the cost is w if the aspect ranks the pair against the observed preference and 0 otherwise, and defaults are 0; Schmitt & Martignon 2006 study the unit-weight version for cue orders. Arbitrary non-negative costs per (item, rule) are a direct generalisation; the correctness argument and the reduction carry over unchanged. With at most two matching rules per item the problem is the linear ordering problem (the cost of an order is a constant plus the weights of the ordered pairs). The DP is also exact for any cost that depends only on the set of rules placed before the capturing rule (Held & Karp 1962; Bodlaender et al. 2012 for vertex-ordering problems). Related but different cost models: in min-sum set cover and pipelined filter ordering an item pays according to the position of the first covering element or the filters evaluated before it is decided, not according to the identity of the capturing rule. Relatives in the dataset: tsp-brute-vs-held-karp and hamiltonian-cycle-count-enumeration-vs-inclusion-exclusion use the same (set, last element) recurrence.
